claims.text: Nearly equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles will have greater thermal stability than traditional alloys.
Nearly equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles will exhibit slower atomic diffusion than traditional alloys.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes a chemically disordered solid solution against phase separation.
High configurational entropy raises the free-energy barrier for phase decomposition.
Atomic-size mismatch produces local strain fields that increase the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
Reduced atomic diffusion kinetically restrains precipitation and phase separation.
Traditional alloys undergo phase separation or precipitation because of thermodynamic instability.
CoCrFeMnNi generally forms a chemically disordered FCC solid solution over a wide temperature range below its solidus at ambient pressure.
CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles with sizes of 5–50 nm can be treated as chemically homogeneous, single-phase FCC particles initially.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles creates a surface-energy driving force that competes with bulk stabilization.
For particles smaller than 10 nm, surface-energy minimization may override configurational-entropy and lattice-distortion stabilization.
The nanoparticles will retain FCC structure and chemical homogeneity to higher temperatures than bulk CoCrFeMnNi of the same composition.
Atomic diffusion coefficients in the nanoparticles will be 2–10 times lower than in traditional alloys at the same temperature.
Particles smaller than 10 nm will exhibit surface segregation of Ni or Mn.
Surface segregation and Ostwald ripening can produce core-shell structures or particle coarsening.

Traditional binary or ternary alloys and bulk HEAs typically undergo phase separation, precipitation, or substantial grain growth above 0.5 Tm because of lower configurational entropy and faster diffusion.
Intrinsic nanoparticle stability fails below approximately 5 nm because surface energy dominates.
Heating beyond the solidus of the most volatile component causes evaporation or rapid surface segregation.
Non-equimolar compositions or impurities may reduce configurational entropy and lower the stability threshold.
Temperature-dependent magnetic fluctuations affect phase stability in CoCrFeMnNi.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome identify particles below 10 nm as the regime where surface effects override intrinsic stability, whereas the boundary field places failure below approximately 5 nm. The distinction between onset of surface effects and actual model failure is not clearly defined.

The mechanism treats high configurational entropy as primarily composition-dependent, yet the baseline broadly attributes instability in bulk HEAs—including the same-composition bulk comparator—to lower configurational entropy. Particle size alone does not explain why a bulk alloy of the same composition would have lower ideal configurational entropy.
